lessons.title: Paying Rent to Your Parents: What Is Allowed and What Gets Checked

body.text: Paying rent to your parents and claiming HRA is legal. Pretending to pay rent to your parents is not. The line between the two is drawn entirely by evidence: ownership, a rent agreement, bank transfers and your parents reporting the rent as their income.

children.text: Lakhs of salaried Indians live in a flat owned by a parent, especially in cities like Pune, Chennai, Hyderabad and Kolkata where families have owned homes for decades. Many have heard the tip: "pay rent to your mother and claim HRA." Sometimes that advice is sound tax planning. Sometimes it is a paper arrangement that falls apart the moment a tax officer asks a few questions. This lesson shows you how to tell which is which.

Nothing in Schedule III (Table: S. No. 11) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 10(13A) of the 1961 Act) or in Rule 279 bars rent paid to a relative. The same tests apply as for any landlord: you receive HRA, you are on the old regime, you actually pay rent for a home you live in, and you do not own that home. Your parent simply becomes your landlord, with the same obligations as any other landlord, including tax on the rent received.

body.label: Rent to parents for HRA
body.value: Allowed, if the arrangement is genuine
body.context: Tax officers and tribunals look past the paperwork to what actually happened: who owns the home, who lives there, whether money really moved, and whether the parent declared it.

children.text: Six Conditions That Make It Genuine

cells: 1. Your parent owns the home, and you do not
You cannot pay rent for a home you own, even partly. If the flat is jointly in your name, the claim fails
Sale deed or property tax receipts in your parent's name
2. You actually live there
The exemption is only for accommodation you occupy
Your address on Aadhaar, bank records and utility bills
3. A written rent agreement
Shows a landlord and tenant relationship with agreed terms, not a family understanding
Signed rent or leave and licence agreement, stamped as required in your state
4. Rent paid by bank transfer or UPI
Proves money actually moved every month
Bank statement showing monthly transfers from your account to your parent's account
5. Your parent reports the rent in their return
The rent you exempt must show up as your parent's income. A mismatch is the single biggest red flag
Your parent's income tax return showing income from house property
6. Rent is at a reasonable market level
Inflated rent looks like a device to maximise the exemption
Listings for similar flats nearby on property portals

body.text: From 1 April 2026, Form 124 asks you to state your relationship with the landlord, and your landlord's PAN is required if total rent in the tax year exceeds ₹1,00,000. So your employer and the tax department will know you pay rent to a parent, and can match your claim against your parent's return using their PAN. Assume every rent-to-parent claim will be cross-checked.

body.title: Quick Check: Spot the Weakest Claim
body.question: Four employees pay rent to a parent. Which claim is most likely to be rejected?
options: Sneha pays her father ₹20,000 a month by UPI for his flat in Kothrud, where she lives, and he declares the rent in his return
Aman pays his mother ₹18,000 a month by bank transfer under a signed agreement, and she files a return showing the rent
Divya hands her mother ₹35,000 in cash each month for a flat in Velachery that is jointly owned by Divya and her mother
Karthik pays his father ₹15,000 a month by NEFT for a flat in Salt Lake his father owns, with a registered agreement
body.explanation: Divya's claim fails on two counts. She is a joint owner of the flat, so she is paying rent partly to herself, and cash payments leave no trail that money actually moved. Rent that is high for the area makes it look worse. The other three have ownership, payment trail and declaration in place.

children.text: How a Claim Falls Apart: A Real Case

In Meena Vaswani v. ACIT, decided by the Mumbai bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal on 30 March 2017 for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12, a chartered accountant claimed HRA exemption for rent paid to her mother. The tribunal called the arrangement a sham and upheld the disallowance.

body.title: Meena Vaswani v. ACIT: the claim vs the findings

columns.label: What she claimed
points: She paid rent to her mother every month
She was entitled to HRA exemption on that rent

columns.label: What the tribunal found
points: She lived in her own larger flat, a few minutes' walk away, with her husband and daughter
Rent was said to be paid in cash, with no matching withdrawals from her bank account
There was no leave and licence agreement
Her mother had not filed returns declaring the rental income

body.text: Notice what sank the claim. It was not the fact that the landlord was her mother. It was that almost every condition failed: she did not live there, no money trail existed, there was no agreement and the income was never declared. Relatives are allowed; fiction is not.

markDefs.definition: Under the house property rules, 30% of the annual value (rent less municipal taxes) is deducted automatically for repairs and upkeep, whatever the actual spend. It is available under both tax regimes.

children.text: A genuine arrangement moves income from you to your parent. You save tax on the exempt HRA. Your parent pays tax on the rent, but only after two reductions under the house property rules in Sections 20 to 25 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Sections 22 to 27 of the 1961 Act): municipal taxes paid, then a flat
on what remains. Whether the family comes out ahead depends on your parent's other income.

Arjun works in Chennai: basic ₹1,00,000 a month, HRA ₹50,000, in the 30% slab under the old regime. He lives in his mother's flat in Anna Nagar and pays her ₹30,000 a month. His exempt HRA is the smallest of ₹6,00,000, ₹3,60,000 minus ₹1,20,000 = ₹2,40,000, and ₹6,00,000, so ₹2,40,000, saving him ₹74,880 in tax. His mother, a retired teacher, pays ₹12,000 a year in property tax and is on the new regime.

body.title: Show me the math for the mother's tax in Scenario B

children.text: Without rent, her taxable income is ₹12,25,000. Tax on slabs is ₹20,000 (5% of ₹4 lakh) plus ₹40,000 (10% of ₹4 lakh) plus ₹3,750 (15% of ₹25,000) = ₹63,750. Because her income is just ₹25,000 above ₹12 lakh, marginal relief limits the tax to that ₹25,000, which becomes ₹26,000 with 4% cess.

With rent, taxable income is ₹14,68,600. Tax is ₹20,000 plus ₹40,000 plus 15% of ₹2,68,600 (₹40,290) = ₹1,00,290. Marginal relief no longer helps, so with cess it is ₹1,04,302. Her tax rises by ₹78,302, more than the ₹74,880 Arjun saves.

body.text: Rent to a parent works best when the parent has little other income and stays within the new regime's zero-tax zone even after adding the rent. When the parent is near or above ₹12 lakh of taxable income, the family can end up paying more in total, even though the arrangement is perfectly legal.

body.title: Try It: Pallavi's Father
body.prompt: Pallavi pays her father ₹25,000 a month for his flat in Aundh, Pune, where she lives. Her father pays ₹8,000 a year in property tax to the Pune Municipal Corporation. What house property income must her father report for the year? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Annual rent is ₹3,00,000. Subtract municipal taxes of ₹8,000 to get ₹2,92,000. The 30% standard deduction is ₹87,600, leaving ₹2,04,400 as income from house property. This is what should appear in his return, and it is what the tax department will look for when Pallavi claims HRA.

body.title: Quick Check: Living Together
body.question: Rahul, 29, lives with his parents in their Hyderabad flat. The family agrees he will "pay rent" of ₹25,000 a month. He transfers it to his father by UPI, but his father uses the same account to pay household bills, including groceries Rahul would otherwise buy. There is a signed agreement and his father declares the rent. What is the main risk?
options: None, because all six conditions are fully met
The claim is automatically invalid because he lives with his parents
The officer may question whether this is rent or simply Rahul's share of household expenses
Rahul must pay GST on the rent
body.explanation: Living in the same home as your parents does not automatically disqualify the claim, and Rahul has the agreement, bank trail and declaration. But when the "rent" is used to run the shared household, an officer may argue it is really a contribution to family expenses, not rent for accommodation. A clear agreement specifying the portion of the home he occupies, consistent monthly payments and rent in line with the market help defend it.

body.title: Scenario: The Round Trip
body.scenario: Nisha lives in her mother's flat in Bandra and transfers ₹50,000 rent to her mother on the 1st of every month. On the 5th, her mother transfers ₹45,000 back to Nisha's account "for her expenses". Her mother files a return declaring the rent. Nisha claims HRA exemption on ₹6,00,000 of rent.
body.prompt: How would a tax officer view this, and what could happen?
body.modelAnswer: The bank statements show the money going to her mother and almost all of it coming back within days. An officer is likely to conclude that only ₹5,000 a month was really paid, or that no genuine rent was paid at all, and that the arrangement exists only to create an exemption. The tribunal in Meena Vaswani treated a less obvious arrangement as a sham. Nisha could lose the exemption, pay the tax with interest, and face a penalty for misreporting income, which can be as high as 200% of the tax on the misreported amount. Her mother's declared rental income does not cure the problem, because the transfers back are visible in both accounts. If the family wants to support Nisha, that should be kept completely separate from rent.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Landlord's Deduction
body.textWithBlank: When a parent earns rent from their child, they can deduct municipal taxes and then a standard deduction of ___% before paying tax on it.
body.explanation: Under the house property rules in Sections 20 to 25 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, 30% of the annual value is deducted for repairs and upkeep. It applies under both regimes, so only 70% of net rent is taxed.

body.title: Rent-to-Parent Evidence File
steps: Confirm the flat is owned only by your parent, and keep a copy of the ownership document
Sign a written rent agreement with your parent and stamp it as required in your state
Set up a monthly bank transfer or UPI payment from your account to your parent's account
Check local listings to confirm the rent is in line with similar flats nearby
Declare the rent and your relationship in Form 124 with your employer, with your parent's PAN if annual rent exceeds ₹1,00,000
Make sure your parent files a return reporting the rent as income from house property, and work out the tax impact for them first
Never route the rent back to your own account

cards.definition: Allowed for HRA exemption when the relative owns the home, you live there, a rent agreement exists, rent is paid through the bank and the relative declares the income.
The head of income under which a landlord reports rent, under Sections 20 to 25 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Sections 22 to 27 of the 1961 Act).
A flat deduction of 30% of annual value (rent less municipal taxes) for a landlord, regardless of actual repair costs, available in both regimes.
Paying rent and receiving most of it back. It suggests the rent was not genuinely paid and can invalidate the exemption.
An arrangement that exists on paper only, as the tribunal found in Meena Vaswani v. ACIT (ITAT Mumbai, 2017), where the exemption was disallowed.

points: The law does not bar rent paid to parents. The usual HRA tests apply, with your parent acting as a genuine landlord
Your parent must own the home, you must live there, and there should be a written agreement and monthly bank payments
Your parent must declare the rent as income from house property, where only 70% of rent after municipal taxes is taxed
Form 124 now asks for your relationship with the landlord, so assume rent-to-parent claims will be cross-checked against your parent's return
Cash payments, joint ownership, inflated rent and money flowing back are the classic red flags that lead to disallowance
Run the family numbers first: if your parent has substantial other income, the family can pay more tax overall

Case references are summarised for teaching and the outcome of any claim depends on its own facts. Provisions reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026 as understood at the time of writing. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
